entries.meaning: Points back at a female subject, or leans on a feminine noun phrase to emphasize it. English drops the reflexive after grooming verbs where many languages keep it — she washed, she dressed, she shaved her legs — so she washed herself is grammatical but sounds like a report from a nursing home rather than ordinary description.
examples: She taught herself to weld from library books. (1)
My mother poured herself a second cup and sat down. (1)
She wasn't thinking about herself when she said that. (1)
Did she hurt herself on the ladder? (1)
The governor herself signed the pardon. (2)
She rebuilt the transmission herself. (2)
Nobody rode with her; she drove all eleven hours by herself. (3)
She was beside herself when the adoption came through. (3)
She hasn't been herself since the layoffs. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ɚˈsɛlf/ · er-SELF — the /h/ drops routinely inside a clause (she hurt 'erself); the stress is on -self in both the reflexive and the intensive use
entries.русский: себя, сама — возвратное и усилительное 3 л. ед. ч. ж. р.; рус. «себя»/«-ся» рода не различает
entries.register: neutral
entries.refers to: a female human antecedent, and in older or affectionate usage a ship, a country, or a named storm. In the reflexive use the antecedent must sit in the same clause: Karen said that Beth cut herself can only mean Beth cut Beth. For a person of unknown or nonbinary gender use themself or themselves.
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own — it is an object, and the verb agrees with the clause's subject. As an intensive it is an appositive and never changes the verb: the senator herself is here, the senators themselves are here.
entries.pattern: [she / female NP] [verb] herself · [she / female NP] [verb] [preposition] herself · [female NP] herself [verb] · [female NP] [verb] [object] herself · by herself · beside herself
entries.contrast: Herself against her: reflexive when the object is the same person as the subject (she cut herself), plain her when it is someone else (he cut her) and when the preposition merely locates something (she pulled the blanket over her, she had the map beside her). Beside herself is the idiom, not the location — it means distraught. Herself can never be a subject: ✗Herself and Diane wrote the grant → Diane and she wrote the grant.
entries.see also: himself, themself, oneself, her, hers, her (determiner)

entries.meaning: Points back at a male subject, or emphasizes a masculine noun phrase. The intensive use is where himself earns its keep in journalism and testimony — the mayor himself signals that the action reached the top of the chain and did not stop at a deputy.
examples: He cut himself shaving and bled onto his collar. (1)
He never forgave himself for missing the flight. (1)
He talks to himself when he's reading contracts. (1)
Why would he do that to himself? (1)
The mayor himself showed up at the ribbon cutting. (2)
He wired the whole garage himself. (2)
He lives by himself out past the reservoir. (3)
He kept the diagnosis to himself for six weeks. (3)
He hasn't been himself since the divorce. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ɪmˈsɛlf/ · im-SELF, and in casual speech /ɪmˈsɛf/ — the /h/ drops inside a clause (he cut 'imself)
entries.русский: себя, сам — возвратное и усилительное 3 л. ед. ч. м. р.; рус. «себя»/«-ся» рода не различает
entries.register: neutral
entries.refers to: a male human antecedent, and occasionally a male animal. In the reflexive use the antecedent must be in the same clause. Generic himself for a person of unspecified sex is dated — every applicant should identify himself now reads as either sexist or archaic; the current choices are themself / themselves, the plural rewrite (applicants should identify themselves), or the heavier himself or herself.
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own. The intensive appositive leaves the verb alone: the author himself admits it.
entries.pattern: [he / male NP] [verb] himself · [he / male NP] [verb] [preposition] himself · [male NP] himself [verb] · [male NP] [verb] [object] himself · by himself · to himself
entries.contrast: Himself against him: reflexive when subject and object are the same man (he blamed himself), plain him when they are not (she blamed him) and after prepositions of place (he closed the door behind him, he had a hundred dollars on him). Against hisself: hisself is the regular formation and the nonstandard one; himself is the irregular form that standard English happens to have kept. And himself is not a subject: ✗John and himself signed → John and he signed.
entries.see also: herself, themself, hisself, him, his, his (determiner)

entries.meaning: The two-sex coordinate reflexive. It is grammatical, unambiguous, and long, which is why it lives on in contracts, statutes, and compliance manuals — where precision outranks rhythm — and why editors of ordinary prose reach for themself or a plural rewrite instead.
examples: No employee may approve a reimbursement to himself or herself. (1)
A defendant has the right to represent himself or herself at trial. (1)
Every applicant should ask himself or herself whether the commute is realistic. (1)
Anyone who is locked out can let himself or herself in with the keypad code. (1)
The policyholder himself or herself must sign the release; a spouse cannot. (2)
A tenant who makes the repair himself or herself may deduct the cost from the rent. (2)
A member may avail himself or herself of the grievance procedure at any time. (3)
A voter who cannot mark the ballot by himself or herself may request assistance at the polling place. (3)

senses.head: Reflexive with a generic or indefinite singular antecedent
body: Each employee must conduct himself or herself professionally.

senses.head: Intensive: emphasis on a generic singular noun phrase, deletable
body: The homeowner himself or herself must sign.

senses.head: In drafted and fixed phrases

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ɪmˈsɛlf ɚ ɚˈsɛlf/ · im-SELF er er-SELF — both /h/s drop inside a clause and or reduces to /ɚ/, so the phrase runs as a string of unstressed syllables around two stressed -selfs
entries.русский: сам или сама, себя — юр./книжн. родонейтральная формула, ныне вытесняемая themself
entries.register: formal — legal, contractual, regulatory, and institutional prose. It was the standard American editorial repair for the generic himself from roughly the mid-1970s to the mid-2010s, and in ordinary writing it now reads as heavy or legalistic.
entries.type: reflexive and intensive pronoun, coordinate phrase
entries.person / number: third person singular, sex-inclusive by coordination — it covers a male referent or a female one, one at a time, and stays singular throughout
entries.refers to: one person of unstated sex, licensed by a singular antecedent in the same clause: a generic noun phrase (each employee, any applicant, the taxpayer) or a singular indefinite (everyone, anybody, whoever). Because the phrase names two sexes and stops, it does not cover a nonbinary referent; for that, and for ordinary modern prose generally, use themself or themselves.
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own, and it does not pluralize its antecedent: each applicant is expected to identify himself or herself, never ✗each applicant are. What usually breaks it is repetition — each employee must submit his or her timesheet himself or herself is grammatical and unreadable, which is the practical argument against the phrase rather than any grammatical one.
entries.pattern: [singular generic NP] [verb] himself or herself · [singular indefinite] [verb] [preposition] himself or herself · [singular NP] himself or herself [verb] · by himself or herself
entries.variants: herself or himself, the same phrase in the other order, common in prose that alternates deliberately · the suspended written form him- or herself, standard in legal drafting · the slashed himself/herself, ordinary on forms and avoided in edited prose · ✗hisself or herself, which drags the vernacular base into the formula
entries.contrast: Against themself and themselves — the same job, one editorial generation apart. Himself or herself is what American style guides recommended once generic himself fell out of favor; after the AP Stylebook and the Chicago Manual of Style both accepted singular they in 2017, the reflexive of choice became themself or themselves, and the coordinate phrase now survives mainly where a document has to track older statutory wording. Against generic himself, which it was built to replace and which reads as dated or sexist today. Against the determiner his or her (each employee must bring his or her badge), which sits in front of a noun and is therefore not a pronoun at all — see his or her (determiner). Three repairs beat the phrase in most sentences: go plural (employees must identify themselves), use singular they (each employee must identify themself), or drop the reflexive altogether (each employee must sign in).
entries.see also: himself, herself, themself, themselves, oneself, his or her (determiner)

entries.meaning: Turns an inanimate or abstract subject back on itself, or emphasizes the thing as opposed to its parts, its copy, or its surroundings. The intensive use is doing real work in technical and legal writing, where the statute itself means the text as enacted and not the commentary around it.
examples: The software updates itself overnight. (1)
History repeats itself, usually with worse actors. (1)
The vine had wrapped itself around the downspout. (1)
The wound won't close itself — it needs stitches. (1)
The house itself is sound; the foundation is not. (2)
The word itself comes from Old Norse. (2)
The lamp switches on by itself every night around nine. (3)
A missed deadline is not, in itself, grounds for termination. (3)
That fact in and of itself proves nothing. (3)

senses.head: Reflexive: a thing acts on itself
Intensive: the thing as opposed to its parts or context

entries.pronunciation note: the /t/ before /s/ is usually unreleased or glottalized, /ɪʔˈsɛlf/, never flapped; there is no weak form, since -self always takes the stress
entries.русский: себя, сам, само — возвратное для предметов и понятий; by itself — сам по себе, автоматически
entries.register: neutral
entries.refers to: an inanimate object, a substance, an abstraction, a process, an animal of unstated sex, an organization or country treated as a singular unit, or a whole preceding situation. It does not refer to a person, except when the person is being deliberately depersonalized. For a group treated as plural use themselves.
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own. As an intensive it keeps the singular verb of its noun: the building itself is sound; contrast the beams themselves are sound.
entries.pattern: [inanimate subject] [verb] itself · [inanimate subject] [verb] [preposition] itself · [noun] itself [verb] · in itself · in and of itself · by itself · of itself
entries.contrast: Itself against it: reflexive when the thing acts on the thing (the system reset itself), plain it otherwise (she reset it). The three fixed phrases are not synonyms — by itself means alone or automatically (the pilot light went out by itself), in itself means intrinsically, considered apart from anything else (the delay isn't fatal in itself), and in and of itself is the emphatic version of in itself, common in American argument and redundant to some editors. Of itself is the older and now bookish variant of in itself (the delay is not, of itself, unreasonable). Against it's: itself has no apostrophe and never contracts.
entries.see also: themselves, oneself, it, its (determiner)

entries.meaning: Points the verb or preposition back at the speaker, or leans on an I already present to emphasize it. Myself is not more polite than me and not more formal than I; the instinct that it is, is exactly what produces the error above.
examples: I burned myself on the oven rack. (1)
I gave myself an extra day to finish the draft. (1)
I don't consider myself an expert on any of this. (1)
I caught myself checking my phone during her toast. (1)
I myself have never voted in a primary. (2)
I hung the drywall myself, badly. (2)
I ate the whole thing by myself and regretted it. (3)
I kept my opinion to myself through the entire meeting. (3)
I haven't felt like myself all week. (3)

Intensive: emphasis on an I already in the clause, deletable

entries.pronunciation note: weak /məˈsɛlf/ · muh-SELF, and in rapid speech /mˈsɛlf/, written informally m'self
entries.русский: себя, сам — возвратное 1 л. ед. ч.; без «I» в том же предложении это ошибка вместо me
entries.register: neutral in its licensed uses; the untriggered use is a marked error in edited American English
entries.refers to: the speaker, and only when the same clause already contains an I — or an understood first-person subject in a clause that has no overt one, as in having taught myself the software, I … or to find myself back here. No first person in the clause means no myself. An imperative is not such a clause: its understood subject is you, which licenses yourself, so ✗Let myself in is not a command anyone can give, while I let myself in is ordinary.
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own. The intensive appositive does not change the verb: I myself have doubts, not ✗I myself has doubts.
entries.pattern: I [verb] myself · I [verb] [preposition] myself · I myself [verb] · I [verb] [object] myself · by myself · to myself
entries.contrast: This is the most common register error in American business English. ✗Please contact myself with any questions → contact me. ✗Bob and myself attended the review → Bob and I attended. ✗The report was prepared by Susan and myself → by Susan and me. Two tests, in order. First, the licensing test: is there an I earlier in the same clause for myself to point back at? If not, myself is wrong. Second, once you know it has to be I or me, take the other person out and listen: Bob and I attended leaves I attended, so Bob and I; contact Bob or me leaves contact me, so Bob or me. The same nerve produces the same two errors with myself nowhere in sight: ✗between you and I and ✗they invited my wife and I are hypercorrections of between you and me and they invited my wife and me, because a preposition or a verb takes the object form however many people are listed. After but, than, as, and as for, myself is common and widely tolerated (no one but myself, as for myself), though conservative editors still change it to me. One honest note on the main error: usage historians point out that and myself coordinations are centuries old and turn up in respectable writers. That has not moved the style guides, and in edited American prose the correction is still made.
entries.see also: ourselves, yourself, me, I, mine, my (determiner)

entries.meaning: The two-word noun phrase that shadows the pronoun oneself — the determiner one's plus the noun self, naming the identity a person has rather than the person a verb points back at. It is entered here for the same reason it's is entered among the possessives: the confusion runs in one direction only, and knowing which word is which settles it.
examples: Solitude can be a threat to one's self as easily as a refuge for it. (1)
The lecture treated one's self as something built rather than something found. (1)
Grief rearranges one's self along with everything else. (1)
A room of one's own turns out to be easier to find than one's self. (1)
The essay distinguishes one's true self from the version one performs at work. (2)
It takes years to forgive one's earlier selves. (3)
Victorian editions print one's self where we now print oneself. (4)
✗ One should always behave one's self at the table. → ✓ behave oneself. (5)

With an adjective between the determiner and the noun
body: one's better self, one's true self

senses.head: In the plural

body: ✗one owes it to one's self → oneself

entries.pronunciation note: two words, two stresses, with the phrase stress on the noun self; there is no weak form, because self here is a full noun and keeps its vowel — contrast the pronoun oneself, one word, stressed wun-SELF
entries.русский: своё «я», своя личность — не местоимение: притяж. one's + существительное self (книжн.)
entries.case: genitive determiner + noun; the phrase as a whole fills a noun slot
entries.register: formal — philosophy, psychology, therapy, and religious writing; it is also the ordinary nineteenth-century printed spelling of the pronoun now written oneself
entries.type: not a pronoun — the possessive determiner one's plus the count noun self
entries.person / number: not applicable — self is an ordinary count noun with the plural selves (one's earlier selves), and the determiner one's belongs to the determiner dictionary. Nothing in the phrase inflects for person.
entries.refers to: a person's identity, character, or psyche — the self as a thing, not a slot pointing back at a subject. It therefore needs no antecedent in its clause, which is the deepest difference between it and oneself: a threat to one's self names something a person has, while one should behave oneself points back at one.
entries.agreement: as a noun phrase it can head a subject and takes a singular verb — one's self is not fixed at twenty — and the plural takes a plural verb: one's earlier selves are embarrassing. The pronoun oneself can do neither, because no reflexive can be a subject.
entries.pattern: one's [adjective] self — one's true self, one's better self · [preposition] one's self · one's selves (plural) · ✗one should behave one's self, where the reflexive slot takes oneself
entries.variants: the same two-word shape runs through the whole paradigm as an ordinary noun phrase — my self, your self, his self, their selves — and none of them is a reflexive. Historically the two-word spelling was also the normal printing of the pronoun itself: through the nineteenth century American books set one's self where a modern editor sets oneself, so in older texts it is a period spelling rather than an error, though reproducing it today looks like one. The vernacular emphatic my own self is the same construction with the emphasizer own wedged in.
entries.contrast: Three tests separate the noun phrase from the pronoun, and all three take one second. First, an adjective can slip in — one's true self, one's better self — and nothing can be inserted into oneself. Second, it pluralizes: one's earlier selves. Third, it can be a subject: one's self changes. When none of the three works, the word wanted is oneself: ✗one should behave one's self, ✗one owes it to one's self. The same split runs one person over between myself and the noun phrase my self, and it is why the emphatic my own self is a phrase rather than a pronoun.
entries.see also: oneself, my own self, myself, one, one's (determiner), own (determiner)

entries.meaning: Serves as the reflexive of generic one. It is the form that lets a writer state a rule about people in general without naming a gender, which is why it survives in ethics, medicine, etiquette, and legal prose while nearly vanishing from conversation.
examples: One cannot expect to change oneself in a weekend. (1)
One owes it to oneself to read the fine print. (1)
It is difficult to make oneself understood over that connection. (2)
Learning to forgive oneself takes longer than forgiving anyone else. (2)
Keeping oneself out of the argument was the wiser course. (2)
There is no shame in dining by oneself. (3)
The trick at these events is simply to be oneself. (3)
One is expected to help oneself to the coffee. (3)

senses.head: Reflexive with generic one
In infinitival and gerundive phrases with no subject
body: to make oneself understood, keeping oneself busy.

entries.pronunciation note: occasionally /ˌwʌnˈsɛlf/ with a secondary stress on the first syllable in careful speech; no weak form
entries.русский: себя, сам — возвратное к обобщённому one; книжн., в формулировках правил «для всех вообще»
entries.register: formal; it belongs to the register that uses generic one at all, and it is rare in American speech
entries.person / number: third person singular, generic and gender-neutral; refers to people in general, including the speaker and hearer
entries.refers to: the generic person named by one in the same clause — one must take care of oneself. It cannot point at a specific individual, and it cannot be licensed by you, he, or they: ✗you should pace oneself → pace yourself.
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own. Its antecedent one takes a singular verb (one is expected to introduce oneself), and American usage keeps the whole chain in one rather than switching to he or they mid-sentence.
entries.pattern: one [verb] oneself · one [verb] [preposition] oneself · [infinitive] oneself (to help oneself) · by oneself · to oneself
entries.contrast: Oneself against one's self: the solid spelling is the pronoun (one should behave oneself); the two-word one's self is a possessive plus the noun self, used only when self means identity or psyche (a threat to one's self). Against yourself: American English overwhelmingly prefers generic you and yourself in speech (you have to pace yourself), reserving one / oneself for formal prose. Two errors to name: ✗one should behave one's self, which puts the noun where the pronoun belongs, and ✗the applicant should ask oneself, which attaches the generic reflexive to a specific subject — repaired as the applicant should ask themself or …himself or herself.
entries.see also: itself, themself, yourself, one, one's (determiner)

entries.meaning: The first person plural reflexive. It carries a small extra load in American English through among ourselves and keep it to ourselves, both of which mark information as staying inside a group.
examples: We taught ourselves enough Spanish to order dinner. (1)
We found ourselves stuck behind a parade. (1)
We shouldn't kid ourselves about the numbers. (1)
We ourselves had no idea the lease was expiring. (2)
We poured the slab ourselves over two weekends. (2)
We had the campground to ourselves until Friday. (3)
We'll sort it out among ourselves. (3)
We were beside ourselves when the results came back clean. (3)

body: by ourselves, among ourselves, to ourselves, beside ourselves.

entries.русский: себя, сами — возвратное 1 л. мн. ч.: «мы сами», «сами себя», «сами по себе»
entries.register: neutral
entries.refers to: the speaker together with at least one other person, licensed by a we or us in the same clause. Both the inclusive we (speaker plus hearer) and the exclusive we (speaker plus others) take ourselves.
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own. The intensive keeps the plural verb of we: we ourselves were surprised, never ✗we ourselves was.
entries.pattern: we [verb] ourselves · we [verb] [preposition] ourselves · we ourselves [verb] · by ourselves · among ourselves · to ourselves
entries.contrast: Ourselves against us: reflexive when subject and object are the same group (we let ourselves in), plain us otherwise (she let us in) and after prepositions of place (we had the whole beach around us). Against ourself: the plural is ourselves in every ordinary use; ourself survives only with the royal or editorial we. And ourselves is never a subject: ✗My wife and ourselves went → my wife and I went, subject case, with the first-person conjunct last. Against each other: we blamed ourselves means the group blamed the group; we blamed each other means the blame went crosswise inside it.
entries.see also: ourself, myself, yourselves, us, we, ours, our (determiner)

entries.meaning: The singular reflexive of singular they. It fills a gap English had left open for centuries — a reflexive for one unnamed person — and it has moved from disputed to standard within a single generation, faster than almost any other change in the pronoun system.

My cousin taught themself to solder from videos. (1)
They don't think of themself as an activist. (1)
Whoever left this note should identify themself. (2)
Anyone can register themself at the front desk. (2)
Someone locked themself out of the server room again. (2)
The witness themself asked to be recalled. (3)
No one who signs up should have to pay for the kit themself. (3)

entries.register: standard and neutral — old in the language but only recently re-established in this use, and some editors still change it to themselves
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral — the reflexive of singular they
entries.refers to: one person whose gender is unknown, unstated, irrelevant, or nonbinary, licensed by a singular they or by a singular indefinite (someone, anyone, each applicant) in the same clause. Not used for plurals: a plural antecedent takes themselves.
entries.agreement: the verb stays plural even though the reference is singular — they consider themself lucky, never ✗they considers. When the antecedent is an indefinite, the indefinite keeps its own singular verb while the reflexive goes -self: everyone is expected to introduce themself. Both halves of that sentence are correct as written.
entries.pattern: they [verb] themself · [singular indefinite] [verb] themself · [singular NP] themself [verb] · by themself
entries.contrast: Themself against themselves is a live split. Both are used for singular they, and both are defensible: Merriam-Webster enters themself as standard, the major American style guides now accept singular they and several allow themself alongside it, and themself is in fact the older of the two — it was the ordinary reflexive of singular they in Middle English, before themselves pushed it aside. Even so, themselves remains more frequent in edited American prose, including with singular reference. The practical rule: match the number of the reference, not the shape of the pronoun — one person, themself; more than one, themselves — and if your editor objects, themselves is the safe fallback. Against himself / himself or herself: themself is now the ordinary American solution to the epicene problem, and himself used generically reads as dated. ✗Themself for a known plural is simply wrong.
entries.see also: themselves, oneself, himself, herself, they, them, theirs, their (determiner)

entries.meaning: The plural reflexive, and the workhorse of the whole class — it covers people, animals, objects, institutions, and a single unnamed person all at once. It also anchors help yourself's plural cousin they helped themselves, which in American English carries a wry secondary sense of taking more than was offered.
examples: The kids let themselves in with the spare key. (1)
The plaintiffs represented themselves at the hearing. (1)
Old barns don't repair themselves. (1)
Everyone at the potluck served themselves twice. (2)
Nobody should have to defend themselves in that tone. (2)
The engineers themselves couldn't explain the failure. (3)
They laid every foot of that tile themselves. (3)
The twins were happy playing by themselves all afternoon. (4)
The numbers speak for themselves. (4)

entries.pronunciation note: weak /əmˈsɛlvz/ · uhm-SELVZ (they hurt 'emselves); a careful citation form is /ðɛmˈsɛlvz/ · them-SELVZ
entries.русский: себя, сами — возвратное 3 л. мн. ч.; также об одном человеке при singular they
entries.register: neutral
entries.person / number: third person plural; also used as a singular with singular they and with singular indefinites
entries.refers to: two or more people, animals, or things, licensed by a plural third-person antecedent in the same clause — and also one person, when the antecedent is singular they or an indefinite like everyone, someone, each applicant. That singular use is standard and is the majority form in edited American prose, though themself is gaining.
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own. The intensive keeps the verb of its noun, so the number of the noun decides: the engineers themselves are unsure, the committee itself is unsure. With a singular indefinite antecedent the verb stays singular while the reflexive is plural in form: everyone is expected to feed themselves.
entries.pattern: [plural subject] [verb] themselves · [plural subject] [verb] [preposition] themselves · [plural NP] themselves [verb] · by themselves · among themselves
entries.contrast: The critical contrast is with each other. They blamed themselves distributes the blame inward — each person blamed that same person; they blamed each other sends it crosswise. The senators contradicted themselves means each was inconsistent; the senators contradicted each other means they disagreed. Against them: reflexive when subject and object are the same group (they helped themselves), plain them otherwise (she helped them) and after prepositions of place (they had the mountains behind them). Against theirselves, which is nonstandard.
entries.see also: themself, each other, one another, theirselves, them, they, theirs

entries.meaning: The second person singular reflexive, and the one that lives inside more fixed expressions than any other pronoun in English: help yourself, behave yourself, make yourself at home, enjoy yourself, suit yourself, be yourself, watch yourself, see for yourself, speak for yourself, pull yourself together, let yourself go, keep it to yourself.
examples: You're going to strain yourself lifting that. (1)
Help yourself to whatever's in the fridge. (2)
Behave yourself at your grandmother's. (2)
You said so yourself on Tuesday. (3)
You yourself signed the amendment. (3)
You can't teach yourself to swim in one afternoon. (4)
Did you drive all the way out here by yourself? (5)
Good to see you — and yourself? (5)
You don't seem yourself today. (5)

Reflexive with an imperative's understood you
Intensive: emphasis on a you already present, deletable
Generic, referring to people in general

entries.pronunciation note: weak /jəˈsɛlf/ · yuh-SELF; a careful citation form is /jʊrˈsɛlf/ · yoor-SELF
entries.русский: себя, сам — возвратное 2 л. ед. ч.; также обобщённо «сам себя», о людях вообще
entries.register: neutral; the untriggered use (could yourself confirm the booking?) is nonstandard
entries.person / number: second person singular — one addressee. For more than one, yourselves.
entries.refers to: the person being addressed, licensed by an overt you or by the understood you of an imperative (help yourself, behave yourself). Also used for the generic you meaning "anyone" — you have to pace yourself — which in American English does the work that oneself does in formal prose.
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own. Second-person you takes a plural verb regardless of number, so both you yourself are responsible (one person) and you yourselves are responsible (several) use are.
entries.pattern: you [verb] yourself · you [verb] [preposition] yourself · you yourself [verb] · [imperative] yourself · by yourself · and yourself?
entries.contrast: Yourself against yourselves is the last surviving number distinction in the English second person: you is both, yourself is one, yourselves is more than one. Against you: reflexive when the addressee acts on the addressee (you'll hurt yourself), plain you otherwise (I'll call you) and after prepositions of place (keep the folder next to you). The untriggered yourself — ✗Could yourself sign here?, ✗The package will be sent to yourself — is the second-person twin of the myself error and just as wrong; the repair is you. The one genuine exception is the elliptical conversational reply and yourself? ("How've you been?" "Good — and yourself?"), which is established American idiom in speech. It does not extend to writing: ✗The package will be sent to yourself is wrong in a letter no matter how polite it feels.
entries.see also: yourselves, myself, oneself, you, yours, your (determiner)

entries.meaning: The second person plural reflexive. Its main practical value is disambiguation — in a language whose you lost its number marking four hundred years ago, yourselves is one of the few places the plural still shows.
examples: You two are going to exhaust yourselves before the hike even starts. (1)
Grab a plate and help yourselves. (2)
Please seat yourselves wherever there's room. (2)
You yourselves voted for this schedule. (3)
Did you frame the whole addition yourselves? (3)
Make yourselves at home; we'll eat around seven. (4)
You'll have to settle this among yourselves. (4)
Were you kids out there by yourselves all afternoon? (4)

entries.pronunciation note: weak /jəˈsɛlvz/; careful /jʊrˈsɛlvz/ · yoor-SELVZ
entries.русский: себя, сами — возвратное 2 л. мн. ч.: показывает множественность, которую «you» уже не различает
entries.register: neutral
entries.person / number: second person plural — two or more addressees
entries.refers to: the group being addressed, licensed by a you (plural) or by the understood you of an imperative directed at several people. The regional and colloquial plural you forms license it too, and all of them take yourselves, never yourself: y'all can seat yourselves (y'all, Southern), you guys can seat yourselves (you guys, general and informal), and — nonstandard — youse (New York City, northern New Jersey, Philadelphia, Boston, Chicago), yinz (Pittsburgh), you'uns (Appalachian).
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own, and you takes a plural verb either way: you yourselves are responsible.
entries.pattern: you [verb] yourselves · you [verb] [preposition] yourselves · you yourselves [verb] · [imperative] yourselves · by yourselves · among yourselves
entries.contrast: Yourselves against yourself: number, and nothing else. Because you is ambiguous, the reflexive is often the only word in the sentence telling you how many people are being addressed — did you make this yourself? is one cook, did you make this yourselves? is a kitchen. Against each other: introduce yourselves means each person gives their own name to the room; introduce yourselves to each other means the introductions go crosswise. Y'all's selves (Southern vernacular) and yourselfs (a regularized plural, general nonstandard) are both nonstandard; the plural of yourself is yourselves, and it stays yourselves whatever plural you form the speaker uses.
entries.see also: yourself, ourselves, themselves, you, yours

entries.meaning: Distributes an action or relation across the members of a plural group so that each member is on both ends of it. The reciprocal is the reason English does not need to say Tom looked at Sue and Sue looked at Tom — Tom and Sue looked at each other carries both directions at once.
examples: The two of them have known each other since kindergarten.
The panelists interrupted each other for a solid hour.
My brother and I text each other about once a week.
They don't speak to each other anymore.
The magnets snapped toward each other the moment I let go.
Do the twins still dress like each other?
Four of the five witnesses contradicted each other.
We promised not to lie to each other about money.
entries.pronunciation note: EECH UTH-er; in connected speech the two words run together as /iˈtʃʌðɚ/ — ee-CHUTH-er, and the final -er is the reduced /ɚ/
entries.русский: друг друга — взаимное местоимение: действие идёт крест-накрест по группе, а не на себя
entries.register: neutral; the more common of the two reciprocals in American English by a wide margin
entries.person / number: invariant in form; requires a plural or coordinated antecedent — they, we, you, the twins, Tom and Sue. It has no singular and no plural of its own: ✗each others.
entries.refers to: the members of a plural antecedent, taken crosswise — every member is both actor and target. Works for people, animals, and things (the two gears mesh with each other). The antecedent must be in the same clause: they said the twins argue with each other can only mean the twins argue.
entries.agreement: it is never a subject, so it triggers no agreement — ✗Each other were late. When each other's + noun does head a phrase, the verb agrees with that noun, not with each other: each other's schedules conflict. Its plural antecedent keeps its own plural verb: the sisters call each other daily.
entries.pattern: [plural subject] [verb] each other · [plural subject] [verb] [preposition] each other · each other's [noun] · ✗each other [verb]
entries.contrast: Against themselves — the contrast that changes the facts of a sentence. The candidates attacked themselves means each was self-critical; the candidates attacked each other means it was a debate. Against one another: the school rule that each other is for exactly two and one another for three or more was invented in the eighteenth century, has never matched usage, and is not enforced by the Chicago Manual, AP, or Merriam-Webster — treat them as interchangeable, with each other the plainer and far more frequent choice. The possessive is each other's, apostrophe before the s: ✗each others, ✗each others'. Using each other as a subject (they know what each other wants) is common in speech and still edited out of formal prose.
entries.see also: each other's, one another, themselves, each, other

entries.meaning: Marks reciprocal possession — what each member of a group has, seen from the others' side. It is one of only two possessives in English built from a two-word pronoun — one another's is the other — which is why the apostrophe placement trips up even careful writers.
examples: The twins finish each other's sentences.
They've been reading each other's email for years, apparently.
We stayed at each other's houses every weekend that summer.
The two firms poached each other's engineers all spring.
The horses stood nose to tail, swishing flies off each other's backs.
They memorized each other's coffee orders within a week.
Neighbors here still watch each other's kids.
The candidates spent the debate quoting each other's worst lines.
entries.русский: друг друга (чей) — притяжательная форма взаимного местоимения, всегда перед существительным
entries.register: neutral
entries.person / number: invariant; requires a plural or coordinated antecedent, exactly as each other does
entries.refers to: the members of a plural antecedent, crosswise, marking what each one possesses relative to the others. It is always followed by a noun — it cannot stand alone the way theirs or hers can: ✗that jacket is each other's.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the noun that follows, never with each other's: each other's names were called; each other's hair was braided. In practice the phrase almost always sits in object position or inside a prepositional phrase, because the reciprocal needs a plural antecedent earlier in the clause to lean on, and a subject has nothing earlier to lean on.
entries.pattern: [plural subject] [verb] each other's [noun] · [plural subject] [verb] [preposition] each other's [noun]
entries.contrast: The apostrophe goes on other, before the s, and the s never moves. Write each other's, never ✗each others and never ✗each others' — other is singular here no matter how many people are involved. The noun after it may be singular or plural and both are standard: they finished each other's sentences and they held each other's hand are equally acceptable — the singular is the natural choice when each person has only one of the thing, the plural when each has several, and neither is an error. Against their: they wrecked their cars leaves open whose car each wrecked; they wrecked each other's cars says the damage went crosswise. Against one another's, which is the same thing in a more formal register.
entries.see also: each other, one another's, theirs, each other's (determiner)

entries.meaning: The formal reciprocal. It means precisely what each other means and differs only in the height of the register, which is why it survives in wedding vows, scripture, bylaws, and treaties while each other does the daily work.
examples: The volunteers helped one another load the truck.
The three agencies routinely blame one another for the delay.
We have promised to care for one another in sickness and in health.
Members of the cohort are expected to review one another's drafts.
The delegations spoke past one another for most of the afternoon.
Neighbors on that street have looked after one another for forty years.
They rarely see one another outside of work.
The two proposals contradict one another on funding.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle syllable is the reduced /ə/ and the stress falls on NUTH; connected speech gives /wʌ nəˈnʌðɚ/
entries.русский: друг друга — то же, что each other, но книжн., в возвышенном или официальном регистре
entries.register: neutral to slightly formal; more common in writing, sermons, ceremony, and legal or diplomatic prose than in conversation
entries.person / number: invariant in form; requires a plural or coordinated antecedent
entries.refers to: the members of a plural antecedent, taken crosswise, exactly as each other does. Used for people far more often than for things — the gears mesh with each other is ordinary, the gears mesh with one another sounds like a manual.
entries.agreement: never a subject, so it triggers no agreement of its own. The plural antecedent keeps its plural verb: the members support one another.
entries.pattern: [plural subject] [verb] one another · [plural subject] [verb] [preposition] one another · one another's [noun]
entries.contrast: Against each other: register, not number. The rule taught in schools — each other for two, one another for three or more — was proposed by eighteenth-century grammarians, was never followed by good writers, and is rejected today by Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and most modern American usage guides. What actually separates them is tone: one another is the more formal and the rarer, and it dominates in fixed elevated phrases (love one another, bear with one another, members of one another). Use either for any number. The possessive is one another's, never ✗one anothers'.
entries.see also: each other, one another's, themselves, another, one

entries.meaning: Marks reciprocal possession in a formal register. Everything true of each other's is true here, one notch up the register scale. ---
examples: The residents look after one another's gardens while they travel.
Committee members are asked to read one another's reports in advance.
The two firms have quietly copied one another's pricing for years.
They learned to respect one another's silences.
Congregants are encouraged to carry one another's burdens.
The delegations rejected one another's opening terms.
The lab groups check one another's calculations before publication.
Old friends forgive one another's worst habits.
entries.русский: друг друга (чей) — притяжательная форма one another; книжн., всегда перед существительным
entries.register: formal; the least frequent of the four reciprocal forms
entries.person / number: invariant; requires a plural or coordinated antecedent
entries.refers to: the members of a plural antecedent, marking crosswise possession. Always followed by a noun; it cannot stand alone.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the following noun, not with one another's: one another's arguments were dismantled. Like each other's, it almost never heads a subject, because the reciprocal needs a plural antecedent earlier in the clause.
entries.pattern: [plural subject] [verb] one another's [noun] · [plural subject] [verb] [preposition] one another's [noun]
entries.contrast: The apostrophe goes on another, before the s — one another's, never ✗one anothers (no apostrophe) and never ✗one anothers' (apostrophe after the s); another stays singular however many people are involved. Against each other's: interchangeable in meaning, with one another's the more formal; in American prose each other's outnumbers it several times over. The following noun may be singular or plural: they respect one another's work and they read one another's drafts are both standard.
entries.see also: one another, each other's, each other, theirs

entries.meaning: The emphatic vernacular intensive. It says what himself says and leans on it — the spoken equivalent of underlining the word — and its solid spelling is one of the oldest signals a writer uses to put a Southern voice on the page.
examples: He hauled every one of those bales his own self. (1; standard: himself)
He built that smokehouse hisownself, back before the war. (1; solid spelling, Southern dialect writing)
The sheriff his own self came out to look at the fence. (2; standard: himself)
She said the governor his own self signed the letter. (2; standard: himself)
He wouldn't hear it from anybody but the old man his own self. (2; standard: himself)
He was sitting out there all by his own self till dark. (3; standard: by himself)

body: He shingled the roof his own self.

senses.head: Appositive beside a masculine noun phrase
body: The preacher his own self came out.

senses.head: Fixed expressions
body: by his own self, all by his own self (alone, unaided).
examples: He hauled every one of those bales his own self. (1; standard: himself)
He built that smokehouse hisownself, back before the war. (1; solid spelling, Southern dialect writing)
The sheriff his own self came out to look at the fence. (2; standard: himself)
She said the governor his own self signed the letter. (2; standard: himself)
He wouldn't hear it from anybody but the old man his own self. (2; standard: himself)
He was sitting out there all by his own self till dark. (3; standard: by himself)

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ɪz oʊn ˈsɛf/ · iz-ohn-SEF — the /h/ drops inside a clause and the final /l/ often goes with it; written solid, hisownself spells the same three syllables run together, /ˌhɪzoʊnˈsɛlf/
entries.русский: сам, самолично — диал./прост. усиленное himself (юг США, Аппалачи, ААВЕ)
entries.case: reflexive; it fills the intensive appositive slot and the object slot after a preposition
entries.register: nonstandard and regional — Southern, South Midland and Appalachian, and African American English, and older rural speech across the country. In print an American meets it almost only in dialogue and literary dialect, where the solid spelling hisownself is a standard way of marking a Southern voice. Not used in edited prose.
entries.type: intensive pronoun phrase — possessive determiner his + the emphasizer own + the noun self
entries.refers to: a male antecedent in the same clause — the same licensing that governs himself, for which this is the emphatic vernacular substitute. The construction is fully productive across the paradigm: my own self, your own self, her own self, our own selves, their own selves, with selves in the plural.
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own; the verb belongs to the clause's subject, exactly as with himself
entries.pattern: [he / male NP] [verb] [object] his own self · [male NP] his own self [verb] · by his own self · all by his own self
entries.variants: the solid spellings hisownself and his ownself, both used in dialect writing to show the phrase said as one word · her own self, your own self, their own selves for the other persons, and my own self, which has its own entry · the Early Modern mine own self, the shape that also gives Shakespeare to thine own self be true
entries.contrast: Against himself: the same slot with the emphasis turned up, and own is what turns it up. Against hisself: hisself substitutes for himself in the plain reflexive slot (he cut hisself), while his own self is overwhelmingly intensive (he shingled it his own self) — two different vernacular moves, usually made by the same speakers. Standard English gets the same emphasis from a bare intensive (he did it himself) or from own in front of a noun (his own truck; see own (determiner)). Recognize it, do not write it: in edited prose the intensive is himself.
entries.see also: himself, hisself, my own self, theirself, theirselves, own (determiner), his (determiner)

entries.meaning: The vernacular masculine reflexive. It is a reliable dialect marker in American speech and in dialogue written to represent it, and it carries strong social stigma in print, which is precisely why a learner needs to be able to identify it and avoid producing it.
examples: He built that whole porch hisself, they say. (vernacular; standard: himself)
He was setting out there by hisself all evening. (vernacular; standard: by himself)
He'd never forgive hisself if that dog got loose. (vernacular; standard: himself)
The old man cut hisself on the fence wire. (vernacular; standard: himself)
He talks to hisself when he's working. (vernacular; standard: himself)
He fixed the tractor hisself, twice. (vernacular intensive; standard: himself)
entries.pronunciation note: iz-SELF or /ɪzˈsɛf/
entries.русский: себя, сам — прост./диал. вместо himself (юг США, Аппалачи, ААВЕ); на письме считается ошибкой
entries.register: nonstandard; Southern, Appalachian, and African American English, and widespread in older rural speech across the country. Marked wrong in any school or workplace writing.
entries.refers to: a male antecedent in the same clause — the same conditions that govern himself, which is the standard equivalent
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own, exactly as himself does
entries.pattern: [he / male NP] [verb] hisself · [male NP] [verb] [object] hisself · by hisself
entries.contrast: Hisself is built the regular way — possessive his + self — matching myself, yourself, ourselves. Standard English instead built the third person from the object forms, giving the irregular himself and themselves, so the nonstandard forms are the ones following the rule. It was ordinary in Middle and Early Modern English and only became a class marker after eighteenth-century grammarians standardized against it. Recognize it, do not write it: the standard form is always himself.
entries.see also: himself, theirself, theirselves, him, his

entries.meaning: The first-person emphatic. It is the most widely used member of the own self family, common in casual speech far outside the South, and the one an American is likeliest to have said out loud without noticing that it is not the written form.
examples: I saw the whole thing my own self, standing right there. (1; standard: myself)
I wouldn't have believed it if I hadn't heard him say it my own self. (1)
I cooked every bit of that dinner my own self. (1)
I'll drive it up there my own self if nobody else will. (1)
I grew up on that road my own self. (1)
I got the truck out of the ditch all by my own self. (2; standard: by myself)
✗ Please forward the invoice to my own self. → ✓ Please forward the invoice to me. (3)

senses.head: Intensive: emphasis on a first-person subject already in the clause
body: I saw it my own self.

senses.head: Fixed expressions
body: by my own self, all by my own self (alone, unaided).

senses.head: Wrong in the untriggered slot, where the plain object pronoun belongs
examples: I saw the whole thing my own self, standing right there. (1; standard: myself)
I wouldn't have believed it if I hadn't heard him say it my own self. (1)
I cooked every bit of that dinner my own self. (1)
I'll drive it up there my own self if nobody else will. (1)
I grew up on that road my own self. (1)
I got the truck out of the ditch all by my own self. (2; standard: by myself)
✗ Please forward the invoice to my own self. → ✓ Please forward the invoice to me. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: weak /mə oʊn ˈsɛlf/ · muh-ohn-SELF — my reduces to /mə/ exactly as it does in myself /məˈsɛlf/, and the dialect spelling myownself shows the same run-together pronunciation
entries.русский: сам, самолично — разг./диал. усиленное myself: «я сам(а) это видел(а)»
entries.register: regional and colloquial — Southern, Appalachian, and African American English, and informal speech well beyond them. Ordinary in conversation and in written dialogue anywhere in the country, out of place in edited prose, where the intensive is myself.
entries.type: intensive pronoun phrase — possessive determiner my + the emphasizer own + the noun self
entries.refers to: the speaker, licensed by an I in the same clause exactly as myself is. Being emphatic, it lands almost always in the intensive slot rather than the plain reflexive one: I saw it my own self is ordinary in speech, while I cut my own self — grammatical enough, but flat where the phrase wants emphasis — is not how speakers actually use it.
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own; the verb agrees with the I that licenses it — I have been out there my own self
entries.pattern: I [verb] [object] my own self · I my own self [verb] (rare, heavily emphatic) · by my own self · all by my own self
entries.variants: the solid spelling myownself in dialect writing · the archaic mine own self, the Early Modern shape behind to thine own self be true · the rest of the paradigm, his own self, her own self, your own self, our own selves, their own selves
entries.contrast: Against myself: the same intensive job with the volume raised, and dialect-marked where myself is not — I built it myself in writing, I built it my own self in speech. Against the noun phrase my self (no own): that is not this construction at all but an ordinary noun about identity, the first-person twin of one's self. And the phrase is no escape from the untriggered-myself error: ✗please forward the invoice to my own self is exactly as wrong as ✗to myself, because the clause has no I in it — the word is me. Recognize it, do not write it: in edited prose the intensive is myself.
entries.see also: myself, his own self, one's self, hisself, me, own (determiner), my (determiner)

entries.meaning: A singular -self form attached to a plural we. It survives in three places: royal proclamation, editorial and institutional prose, and dialect where it simply replaces ourselves. Only the first two are defensible in writing, and both are rare enough that most American readers will read it as a typo.
examples: We have asked ourself whether the paper served its readers well. (editorial we)
We shall reserve the decision to ourself. (royal we)
The board must ask ourself what obligation we owe the members. (corporate we; many editors would write ourselves)
We find ourself in an unfamiliar position. (editorial we)
We let ourself in with the key under the mat. (nonstandard for ourselves)
We had the cabin to ourself all weekend. (nonstandard for ourselves)
entries.pronunciation note: ow-er-SELF
entries.русский: себя, сами — устар./книжн. при «королевском» или редакционном we; иначе прост. вместо ourselves
entries.register: split — archaic and formal with the royal or editorial we; nonstandard as a substitute for ourselves
entries.person / number: first person, grammatically plural we referring to a single entity — a monarch, an editorial board speaking as one voice, or a collective treated as one body
entries.refers to: the single person or single corporate entity denoted by a plural we. It is licensed only when we means one: we have asked ourself whether the paper went too far (an editorial board). With an ordinary plural we it is an error: ✗my wife and I let ourself in → ourselves.
entries.agreement: we keeps its plural verb even in the royal and editorial senses — we are not amused, never ✗we is
entries.pattern: we [verb] ourself (with singular reference only) · [imperative or infinitive with collective we] ourself
entries.contrast: Ourselves is the form in every ordinary use. Ourself is legitimate only where we is a plural of majesty or a corporate singular, and even there some usage panels reject it. Note the mirror-image logic with themself: both are plural-shaped pronouns given a -self singular ending to match singular reference, and themself has won broad acceptance while ourself has not — because singular they is a living construction and the royal we is not. Outside those narrow contexts, ourself for ourselves is nonstandard.
entries.see also: ourselves, themself, theirself, we, us

entries.meaning: The vernacular singular reflexive. It deserves its own entry rather than a footnote, because it is the word standard English spent a century hunting for — a -self form for one unnamed person — reached from the other direction and stigmatized for its base rather than for its logic.
examples: Somebody locked theirself out of the truck again. (vernacular; standard: themself or themselves)
Anybody could hurt theirself on that bottom step. (vernacular; standard: themself)
Nobody around here has to explain theirself twice. (vernacular; standard: themself)
He said whoever took it can keep it to theirself. (vernacular; standard: themself)
The new hire drove all the way out here by theirself. (vernacular; standard: by themself)
They wired that whole shed theirself, they told me. (vernacular intensive; standard: themself)
entries.pronunciation note: thair-SELF; in fast speech the first syllable reduces to /ðɚ/ — thur-SELF
entries.русский: себя, сам(а) — прост./диал. вместо themself, об одном человеке
entries.register: nonstandard; Southern, Appalachian, and African American English, and older rural speech generally — the singular partner of theirselves
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral, where standard English uses themself or themselves
entries.refers to: one person, named in the same clause by a singular indefinite (somebody, anybody, everybody, nobody, whoever) or by singular they. The licensing conditions are exactly those of the standard forms; only the base of the word is different.
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own. The indefinite antecedent keeps its own singular verb — somebody was locked out — precisely as it does with standard themself, and singular they keeps its plural verb — they were locked out.
entries.pattern: [singular indefinite] [verb] theirself · they [verb] theirself · [singular indefinite] [verb] [preposition] theirself · by theirself
entries.contrast: Theirself and standard themself are two different words solving the same problem from two different bases — the vernacular builds on the possessive their, standard English on the object form them — and the vernacular one is the more regular of the two, matching myself, yourself, ourselves. It is still the one that gets marked wrong. Against theirselves: number and nothing else, one person against a group; vernacular speakers hold that line more consistently than standard English holds the themself / themselves line. Against hisself: same nonstandard pattern, different person and gender. Recognize it, do not write it: the standard forms are themself for one person and themselves for a group — and themselves is also standard for one person.
entries.see also: theirselves, themself, themselves, hisself, they, them

entries.respell: thair-SELVZ; the singular variant theirself is /ðɛrˈsɛlf/
entries.meaning: The vernacular plural reflexive. It is common in American speech and in written dialogue representing it, and stigmatized everywhere else.
examples: They painted the whole house theirselves. (vernacular; standard: themselves)
The kids got theirselves into trouble at the creek. (vernacular; standard: themselves)
They were out there by theirselves half the night. (vernacular; standard: by themselves)
Folks around here look after theirselves. (vernacular; standard: themselves)
They helped theirselves to the last of the pie. (vernacular; standard: themselves)
The girls sewed every one of those costumes theirselves. (vernacular intensive; standard: themselves)
entries.pronunciation note: thair-SELF
entries.русский: себя, сами — прост./диал. вместо themselves
entries.register: nonstandard; Southern, Appalachian, and African American English, and older rural speech generally
entries.person / number: third person plural; the singular partner is theirself, which has its own entry
entries.refers to: a plural third-person antecedent in the same clause — the same conditions that govern themselves, which is the standard equivalent
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own, exactly as themselves does
entries.pattern: [plural subject] [verb] theirselves · [plural subject] [verb] [preposition] theirselves · by theirselves
entries.contrast: Like hisself, theirselves is the regular formation — possessive their + selves, matching ourselves and yourselves — while standard themselves is built from the object form them. The nonstandard form is the consistent one; the standard form is the exception. Recognize it, do not write it: the standard forms are themselves for a plural antecedent and themself or themselves for a singular one. Note that standard themself and nonstandard theirself are different words solving the same problem from different bases.
entries.see also: themselves, themself, theirself, hisself, them, theirs

entries.meaning: The subject-base reflexive of singular they, and the newest and rarest of the three they-family -self forms. It has no dictionary, no style guide, and no dialect tradition behind it, which sets it apart from the vernacular forms above: those are stigmatized for their base, this one is simply not established.
examples: Somebody locked theyself out of the studio again. (nonstandard; standard: themself or themselves)
Anyone can register theyself at the front desk. (nonstandard; standard: themself)
They don't think of theyself as a beginner anymore. (nonstandard; standard: themself)
Whoever wrote this note should identify theyself. (nonstandard; standard: themself)
My roommate taught theyself to knit over the winter. (nonstandard; standard: themself)
They drove all the way to Tucson by theyself. (nonstandard; standard: by themself)
They put up that whole fence theyself. (nonstandard intensive; standard: themself)
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ðəˈsɛlf/ · thuh-SELF — reduced, it stands one nasal away from the everyday fast-speech themself /ðəmˈsɛlf/, close enough that the two blur in running speech and are separated far more reliably on the page than in the ear
entries.русский: себя, сам(а) — неологизм, нестанд. вариант themself; в словари не входит
entries.register: nonstandard and rare — met chiefly in informal online writing and in speech since the 2010s. No major American dictionary enters it, and editors treat it as an error; the standard form it reaches for is themself.
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral — a reflexive of singular they, built on the subject form
entries.refers to: one person whose gender is unknown, unstated, irrelevant, or nonbinary, licensed by a singular they or by a singular indefinite (someone, anyone, whoever, each applicant) in the same clause — the same conditions that govern themself. A plural antecedent takes themselves; ✗theyselves is not a form anyone uses.
entries.agreement: carries no verb agreement of its own. Singular they keeps its plural verb — they were locked out, never ✗they was — and a singular indefinite antecedent keeps its own singular verb: somebody is going to hurt theyself.
entries.pattern: they [verb] theyself · [singular indefinite] [verb] theyself · [singular NP] theyself [verb] · by theyself
entries.contrast: Three bases, one job. Standard themself is built on the object form them, vernacular theirself on the possessive their, and theyself on the subject form they — and the subject form is the one base English uses for no reflexive at all: there is no ✗heself, ✗sheself, ✗weself, ✗Iself. That is why theyself reads as an error even to readers who accept themself without blinking, and it is the reason this form has stayed rare while themself went standard inside a single generation. It is also a recent formation rather than an inherited one — unlike hisself and theirselves, which are centuries old and carry a regional history, theyself is what a writer produces by attaching -self to the pronoun actually spoken. Recognize it, do not write it: the standard forms are themself for one person and themselves for a group — and themselves is standard for one person too.
entries.see also: themself, themselves, theirself, theirselves, hisself, they, them

entries.meaning: The archaic second person singular reflexive. It is worth knowing because it appears in the most quoted sentences in English — know thyself, love thy neighbor as thyself, physician, heal thyself — and because those quotations are still used in ordinary modern American speech. ---
examples: Know thyself. (inscribed at Delphi, and quoted ever since)
Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself.
Physician, heal thyself.
Thou knowest thyself better than any counselor could.
Trouble not thyself over what cannot be mended.
Gird thyself, for the road is long.
entries.pronunciation note: the th is voiced /ð/, as in this, not the voiceless th of thin
entries.русский: себя, сам — устар. возвратное к thou; ныне лишь в высоком стиле: «познай самого себя»
entries.register: archaic; found now only in scripture, hymns, Shakespeare, oaths, mottoes, and deliberate period style
entries.person / number: second person singular, familiar — the reflexive of thou / thee / thy
entries.refers to: a single addressee, in the intimate or familiar register that thou marked before English collapsed the second person into you. The modern equivalent is yourself.
entries.agreement: takes no verb agreement of its own; its antecedent thou took the old -est ending on the verb (thou knowest thyself)
entries.pattern: thou [verb-est] thyself · [archaic imperative] thyself (know thyself) · to thine own self (the thine + noun variant)
entries.contrast: Thyself against yourself: the same slot, four hundred years apart. Against the Shakespearean thine own self (to thine own self be true), which is not the pronoun at all but the possessive thine plus the noun self — an important distinction, because ✗thineself as one word is a modern invention with no historical basis. Thyself goes with thou; pairing it with you (✗you should know thyself) is a common mistake in mock-archaic writing.
entries.see also: yourself, oneself, thy (determiner), thine (determiner)

entries.meaning: The reflexive of the ae set. It is the neopronoun likeliest to slip past an American ear rather than an American eye, because every pronunciation it has lands on or beside a word the language already uses.
examples: Ae taught aerself to throw pots out of a library book. (1)
Ae poured aerself the last of the coffee and kept reading. (1)
Ae doesn't count aerself among the regulars yet. (1)
Ae rewired the whole kiln shed aerself. (2)
The treasurer aerself asked for the audit. (2)
Ae drove out to the coast by aerself in February. (3)
Ae kept the news to aerself until the offer was signed. (3)

entries.register: neutral among the speakers who use the set, and rare in general American writing — the reflexive of the ae / aer / aers set, one of the sets that spread through pronoun-listing sites and online profiles from the early 2010s on. Used by a small number of speakers; American dictionaries do not enter it, and a reader met with it in print will usually have seen it introduced first.
entries.refers to: one person who uses the ae set, named in the same clause. Aer serves as both the object form and the possessive determiner (I called aer, aer brother), so the reflexive has a single base and no competing spelling of the kind xemself and nemself show.
entries.agreement: ae takes a singular verb — ae is on the schedule, ae has already answered, ae was the first one here. The reflexive carries no agreement of its own and is always -self, never -selves.
entries.pattern: ae [verb] aerself · ae [verb] [preposition] aerself · [NP] aerself [verb] · by aerself
entries.contrast: Against the Spivak variant eirself: the two are homophones for most speakers, /ɛrˈsɛlf/ both, and only the spelling and the subject pronoun — ae against e or ey — tell them apart. Against herself: the same collision one step further along, since unstressed herself is /ɚˈsɛlf/ and aerself reduces to the same thing. Against emself, coself, faerself, hirself, nemself, perself, verself, xemself, and zirself: separate sets, not substitutes for one another. Against themself: singular both, but ae takes a singular verb where singular they takes a plural one.

entries.meaning: The reflexive of the co set, the oldest of these coinages — it predates the z- and x- forms by two decades — and the only one with a documented institutional home, in the bylaws and daily speech of a Virginia commune.
examples: Co taught coself to keep bees the first summer here. (1)
Co signed coself up for two extra kitchen shifts. (1)
Co doesn't think of coself as anybody's supervisor. (1)
Co framed the whole sleeping loft coself. (2)
The membership clerk coself read the bylaw aloud. (2)
Co walked back from the garden by coself in the dark. (3)
Co kept the decision to coself until the meeting. (3)

Rare outside that world and outside writing about it.
entries.refers to: one person who uses the co set, named in the same clause. Co is the same word in the subject and the object slot (co called, I called co), the way you is, so the possessive cos and the reflexive coself are the only separate forms in the set — the shape perself has too.
entries.agreement: co takes a singular verb — co is on kitchen shift, co has signed the sheet, co was at the meeting. The reflexive is -self, never -selves.

examples: Ey taught eirself to read a wiring diagram over one winter. (1)
Ey gave eirself the weekend off after the launch. (1)
Ey doesn't count eirself among the founders, whatever the filing says. (1)
Ey introduced eirself to the room and wrote the pronouns on the whiteboard. (1)
E wired the entire booth eirself the night before the show opened. (2)
The archivist eirself pulled the box out of storage for us. (2)
Ey rode out to the trailhead by eirself and camped two nights. (3)
Ey kept the offer to eirself until the paperwork cleared. (3)

entries.register: neutral among the speakers who use the set, and rare in general American writing — the reflexive of the Spivak set e (or ey) / em / eir / eirs, named for the mathematician Michael Spivak, whose typesetting writing used the forms, and spread through LambdaMOO and other text-based online communities in the 1990s. It is not part of the inherited English paradigm and is not used by most American speakers; among speakers who use a gender-neutral pronoun at all, singular they is by a wide margin the commoner choice. No general American dictionary enters it, and the major style guides neither endorse nor rule it out — AP and Chicago both tell a writer to use the forms a person uses and to gloss an unfamiliar one once for readers who will not recognize it. In practice the set is introduced by the person who uses it, in a profile line, an email signature, or an introduction round, and that is what settles which form a writer should use.
entries.type: reflexive and intensive pronoun; the possessive-base form of the Spivak set, beside the object-base emself
entries.refers to: one person who uses the Spivak set, named in the same clause by e / ey or by a noun phrase. The set inflects in full: subject e or ey, object em, possessive determiner eir, possessive pronoun eirs, reflexive emself or eirself. Eirself is the member built on the possessive, the way myself and yourself are; emself is built on the object, the way himself and themself are. Licensing is ordinary reflexive licensing — the antecedent must sit in the same clause, exactly as himself needs its he.
entries.agreement: the subject takes a singular verb — ey is on the list, e has already voted, ey was hired in March — where singular they keeps the plural (they are here). The reflexive carries no agreement of its own, and it is always -self, never ✗eirselves, because it names one person.

entries.variants: emself, the object-base form, which has its own entry below and is the more frequently listed of the two; speakers differ on which they take, and a person's own choice settles it. The split is structurally the same one standard themself (object base them) makes against vernacular theirself (possessive base their), and the same one xemself makes against xyrself and nemself against nirself — with the difference that neither Spivak form carries stigma.
entries.contrast: Against emself: the same set and the same person, two bases and two pronunciations — /ɛrˈsɛlf/ against /ɛmˈsɛlf/ — and neither is a correction of the other. Against aerself: a homophone from a different set, /ɛrˈsɛlf/ both, so only the spelling and the subject pronoun — e / ey against ae — separate them on the page, and nothing separates them in speech. Against herself: unstressed herself is /ɚˈsɛlf/, which is exactly where reduced eirself lands. Against themself: both name one person and neither marks gender, but the verb splits them — ey is here, they are here. Against xemself, zirself, hirself, coself, faerself, nemself, perself, and verself: separate sets, not substitutes for one another, and reaching for the wrong set is the same order of mistake as using the wrong name.

entries.register: neutral among the speakers who use the set, and rare in general American writing — the reflexive of the fae / faer / faers set, built on the noun fae (a fairy) and circulated on Tumblr and other social platforms from the mid-2010s on. It is the most frequently cited of the nounself pronouns — sets drawn from an existing noun rather than from an invented syllable — and is used by a small number of speakers.
entries.refers to: one person who uses the fae set, named in the same clause. Faer is both the object form and the possessive determiner (I met faer, faer roommate), so there is one base and one spelling of the reflexive.
entries.agreement: fae takes a singular verb — fae is presenting second, fae has the keys, fae was hired in June. The reflexive is -self, never -selves.
entries.pattern: fae [verb] faerself · fae [verb] [preposition] faerself · [NP] faerself [verb] · by faerself
entries.contrast: Against aerself, one consonant away in speech and a separate set. Against the ordinary noun fae and the adjective fair, which the forms collide with — a reader meeting the set cold can hear a common word where a pronoun was meant, which is why writers who use it in print usually gloss it once. Against emself, coself, hirself, nemself, perself, verself, xemself, and zirself: separate sets, not substitutes for one another. Against themself: singular both, and again the verb splits them — fae is here, they are here.
entries.see also: aerself, coself, emself, nemself, perself, themself, fae / faer

entries.meaning: The reflexive of the ze/hir set, the oldest of the z- pronouns and the one most often met in writing from the 1990s and 2000s.
examples: Ze taught hirself to read music at forty. (1)
Ze poured hirself a cup and went back to the reading. (1)
Ze doesn't describe hirself as an activist. (1)
Ze built every one of those shelves hirself. (2)
The editor hirself called to ask about the footnote. (2)
Ze drove the whole way up to the cabin by hirself. (3)
Ze kept the news to hirself for a month. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: also /hɚˈsɛlf/ · her-SELF for speakers who say hir like her, which makes it a homophone of herself; weak /ɪrˈsɛlf/ — the /h/ drops inside a clause exactly as it does in himself and herself
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — возвратное набора ze/hir
entries.register: neutral among the speakers who use the set, and rare in general American writing — the reflexive of the ze (also spelled zie or sie) / hir / hirs set, which circulated in queer, academic, and Usenet writing from the early 1990s. Still in use, though less than ze/zir and far less than singular they.
entries.refers to: one person who uses the ze/hir set, named in the same clause. Hir serves as both the object form and the possessive determiner (I called hir, hir car), so the reflexive has only one possible base and there is no competing spelling of the kind xemself shows.
entries.agreement: ze takes a singular verb — ze is waiting, ze was the first to sign, ze has two kids. The reflexive is -self, never -selves.
entries.pattern: ze [verb] hirself · ze [verb] [preposition] hirself · [NP] hirself [verb] · by hirself
entries.contrast: Against herself: for speakers who pronounce hir as /hɚ/ the two words are homophones and only the spelling separates them, which is one reason the z- spellings have gained ground. Against zirself: the same subject pronoun ze heads both sets, and what differs is the object and possessive form (hir against zir), so the reflexive is often the clearest signal of which set a writer is using. Against themself: singular either way, but ze takes a singular verb and singular they a plural one.

entries.meaning: The reflexive of the ne set. It is the plainest of the n- forms and the one most easily lost in speech, since its reduced shape sits a single consonant away from the reduced themself an American hears every day.
examples: Ne taught nemself statistics out of a used textbook. (1)
Ne gave nemself until Friday to finish the draft. (1)
Ne doesn't consider nemself a morning person. (1)
Ne ran every one of those samples nemself. (2)
The reviewer nemself asked to see the raw data. (2)
Ne flew out to the conference by nemself. (3)
Ne kept the result to nemself until the lab confirmed it. (3)
Ne found nirself fielding the same question all week. (1; the possessive-base variant)
